messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (Settled mean output)
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (Maximum voltage)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (Ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (Cold start)
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (Settled steady state)
    *   Piezo characteristics: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (S1).
    *   Operating conditions (S1-S6) vary $I_p, f, C_p, R_L,$ and temperature.
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, 4 switches, 2 SYNC controllers.

    *   The FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) failed on several fronts:
        *   S2: Ripple, Startup, Settled.
        *   S3: $V_{max}$ (Too high).
        *   S4: $V_{avg}$, Ripple, Startup, Settled.
        *   S5: $V_{avg}$, Startup.
        *   S6: $V_{avg}$, Startup.
    *   The main problems are:
        *   Inefficient energy extraction (low $V_{avg}$ for heavy loads).
        *   Lack of voltage regulation (too high $V_{max}$ for light loads).
        *   Slow startup for low-frequency/high-load cases.

    *   *Passive Full-Bridge (FBR):* Too simple, inefficient, no regulation.
    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* Significantly improves extraction efficiency by inverting the voltage across $C_p$ at the extrema.
    *   *SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction):* Another high-efficiency technique, but typically requires more complex switching.
    *   *Voltage Regulation:* Since $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ and we need a stable $1.8\text{ V}$, a Zener clamp or a more sophisticated buck-converter/regulator is needed. However, we only have basic components (S, D, L, C). A DZ33 zener diode can act as a clamp to prevent $V_{max}$ from exceeding $3.3\text{ V}-3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Parallel) with FBR and Zener Clamp.**
        *   SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to flip the charge on $C_p$ every half-cycle.
        *   The charge then flows through a rectifier into the storage capacitor.
        *   Structure: Piezo -> FBR -> $C_{out}$. Add SSHI flip circuit (L and S) across the piezo terminals.
        *   Wait, the standard SSHI flip is across the piezo. $S$ closes at the peaks.
        *   Circuit:
            - Piezo: $pzp, pzn$.
            - Rectifier: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$ (Wait, that's a standard FBR, but $pzp/pzn$ are AC).
            - Better Rectifier: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$ - No, a full bridge is: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$ is wrong.
            - Correct Full Bridge: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$? No.
            - Standard Bridge: Node A ($pzp$), Node B ($pzn$), Node C ($out$), Node D ($0$).
                - $D_1: pzp \to out$
                - $D_2: pzn \to out$
                - $D_3: 0 \to pzp$
                - $D_4: 0 \to pzn$
            - This is a standard FBR. To add SSHI: An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
            - $S$ closes at $V_{pzp}$ extrema. $S$ is between $pzp$ and $pzn$ via $L$? No, usually $L$ is in series with $S$.
            - SSHI: Switch $S$ connects $pzp$ to $pzn$ through $L$. This inverts $V_{Cp}$.
            - $S$ triggers at "both" edges.

    *   **Design 2: Half-Bridge SSHI (or modified version).**
        *   If $V_{oc}$ is around 3.2V, a full bridge might have too many diode drops (2 $\times$ 0.25V = 0.5V), leaving only 2.7V.
        *   A half-bridge rectifier (using $pzn$ as ground) is more efficient but requires a symmetric piezo source. Our source is between $pzp$ and $pzn$.

    *   **Design 3: Zener Clamped FBR with larger $C_{out}$.**
        *   The FBR failed $V_{max}$ on S3. A DZ33 zener on `out` will clamp it.
        *   The FBR failed $V_{avg}$ on S4, S5, S6. This suggests we need better energy extraction.

    *   Piezo: $pzp, pzn$.
    *   Rectifier (FBR):
        - $D_1: pzp \to out$
        - $D_2: pzn \to out$
        - $D_3: 0 \to pzp$
        - $D_4: 0 \to pzn$
    *   SSHI flip:
        - $L_1: pzp \to n1$
        - $S_1: n1 \to pzn$
        - $SYNC G_1: edges=both, phase=0, ton \approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   Storage: $C_{out}: out \to 0$.
    *   Clamp: $D_{zener}: 0 \to out$ (Model DZ33).
    *   Wait, $S_1$ should be at the peaks. $G_1$ closes at "both" edges (zero crossings of current).
    *   Let's check the $V_{max}$ limit. 3.6V. DZ33 clamps at 3.3V. This is perfect.

    *   $L = 1\text{ mH} \dots 10\text{ mH}$.
    *   $C_{out} = 1\text{ uF} \dots 10\text{ uF}$.
    *   $T_{on} = \pi\sqrt{L C_p} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-3} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$. (The limit for $t_{on}$ is $1\text{ ms}$, so this fits).

    *   S1: $I_p=50\text{u}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=330\text{k}$.
    *   S2: $I_p=25\text{u}, f=50\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=680\text{k}$.
    *   S3: $I_p=100\text{u}, f=200\text{Hz}, C_p=17.5\text{nF}, R_L=4700\text{k}$. (Light load $\to$ high $V_{out} \to$ needs Zener).
    *   S4: $I_p=25\text{u}, f=50\text{Hz}, C_p=32.5\text{nF}, R_L=1000\text{k}$.
    *   S5: $I_p=100\text{u}, f=200\text{Hz}, C_p=32.5\text{nF}, R_L=150\text{k}$. (Heavy load $\to$ needs high efficiency).
    *   S6: $I_p=50\text{u}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=200\text{k}$. (Heavy load $\to$ needs high efficiency).

    *   SSHI is the standard for high-efficiency piezo harvesting. It significantly boosts the voltage before rectification.
    *   The Zener clamp handles the over-voltage.
    *   $C_{out}$ handles the ripple.

    *   $D_1$: pzp -> out (DSCH)
    *   $D_2$: pzn -> out (DSCH)
    *   $D_3$: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
    *   $D_4$: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    *   $D_z$: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    *   $C_{out}$: out -> 0 (2.2uF)
    *   $L_1$: pzp -> n1 (10mH)
    *   $S_1$: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G1)
    *   $G_1$: SYNC (ton=1.5e-4, edges=both, phase=0)

    Wait, if I use a full bridge and an SSHI flip across the piezo, is that optimal?
    The SSHI flip (S and L) effectively creates a voltage spike at the peaks. The FBR then captures this.

    Another option: A "Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor" (SSHI) usually flips the voltage across the capacitor *before* it goes through the rectifier. This is exactly what I described.

    Wait, is there a simpler way?
    What if we just use a Zener clamp on the FBR?
    S3 would pass. S4, S5, S6 still fail $V_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$.
    So we definitely need the L-S flip (SSHI) to increase energy extraction.

    *   S1-S6 cover a wide range of loads.
    *   Heavy loads (S5, S6) need $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Light loads (S3) need $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   $C_{out}$ needs to be large enough for ripple $\le 0.05\text{ V}$. $2.2\text{ uF}$ might be okay, but maybe $10\text{ uF}$ is safer.

    Let's check $C_{out}$ ripple: $\Delta V = I_{load} / (f \cdot C_{out})$.
    For S1: $I_{load} = 2.2\text{ V} / 330\text{ k}\Omega \approx 6.6\text{ uA}$.
    $f = 100\text{ Hz} \cdot 2$ (rectified) = $200\text{ Hz}$.
    $\Delta V = 6.6\text{ uA} / (200 \cdot 2.2\text{ uF}) \approx 15\text{ mV}$. (Ok).
    For S2: $I_{load} = 2\text{ V} / 680\text{ k}\Omega \approx 3\text{ uA}$. $f=100\text{ Hz}$.
    $\Delta V = 3\text{ uA} / (100 \cdot 2.2\text{ uF}) \approx 13\text{ mV}$. (Ok).
    Wait, S2 FBR ripple was $83\text{ mV}$. Why?
    Ah, $C_{out}$ might be too small, or the energy delivered per cycle is very low.
    $I_p$ is only $25\text{ uA}$ in S2.

    Let's try a slightly larger $C_{out}$ for the SSHI design, e.g., $4.7\text{ uF}$.

    Is there any other topology?
    Maybe a "buck-boost" like structure using the SYNC?
    But we have very limited components.
    The SSHI is the most robust high-efficiency topology for this.

    Let's refine the SSHI bridge:
    $D_1: pzp \to out$
    $D_2: pzn \to out$
    $D_3: 0 \to pzp$
    $D_4: 0 \to pzn$
    $S_1: pzp \to n1$
    $L_1: n1 \to pzn$
    $G_1: ton=1.5e-4, edges=both, phase=0$
    $C_{out}: out \to 0$
    $D_z: 0 \to out$

    Wait, look at the reference FBR:
    $D_1: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]$
    This is exactly the FBR I planned.

    Wait, one detail: $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$. SSHI helps significantly with startup because it extracts more energy per cycle.

    One more thing: The SYNC controller cost is $0.5\text{ uA}$.
    S2: $I_{load} \approx 3\text{ uA}$. Cost is $0.5\text{ uA}$. Not a huge deal.
    S4: $I_{load} = 1.8\text{ V} / 1000\text{ k}\Omega = 1.8\text{ uA}$. Cost is $0.5\text{ uA}$. Still okay.

    What if $S_1$ closes *before* the peak?
    Phase can be adjusted. $0.0$ is the extrema.
    The energy extraction is maximized when the switch closes exactly at the peak of the voltage (which is the zero crossing of the current).

    Is there any other structure?
    Maybe a "Charge Pump" style? No, the SYNC controllers are better used for SSHI.

    Let's double check the $C_{out}$ value.
    S4 had $V_{avg}=1.79\text{V}$ and $t_{up}=0.759\text{s}$.
    SSHI should push $V_{avg}$ up and $t_{up}$ down.

    Check $V_{max}$ for S3:
    S3 has $R_L = 4700\text{ k}\Omega$. It's very light.
    $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$.
    Without the Zener, $V_{out}$ will climb to $V_{oc} - 2\text{V}_{diode} \approx 2.7\text{ V}$?
    Wait, why did the reference FBR get $4.2\text{ V}$ for S3?
    Ah, $I_p = 100\text{ uA}$, $f = 200\text{ Hz}$, $C_p = 17.5\text{ nF}$.
    $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) = 100\text{ uA} / (2\pi \cdot 200 \cdot 17.5\text{ nF}) = 100\text{u} / 22\text{n} \approx 4.5\text{ V}$.
    So $V_{max}$ would be around $4\text{ V}$, which exceeds $3.6\text{ V}$.
    The DZ33 zener clamp is essential.

    Actually, instead of $L$ and $S$ in series, some SSHI versions use different configs. But $L$ in series with $S$ across the piezo is the standard "Parallel-SSHI".

    Wait, let me reconsider the bridge.
    If we use a half-bridge, we save one diode drop.
    But the piezo is not grounded. To use a half-bridge, we'd need to ground $pzn$.
    But $pzn$ is part of the piezo model.
    Wait, the test bench says the piezo is between $pzp$ and $pzn$.
    If I connect $pzn$ to $0$, it's basically a half-bridge.
    But the piezo is a current source $I_p \sin(\dots)$ in parallel with $C_p$.
    If $pzn$ is connected to $0$, then $pzp$ will swing positive and negative.
    A half-bridge rectifier would then be:
    $D_1: pzp \to out$
    $D_2: 0 \to pzp$ (No, that's not right).
    Half bridge:
    $D_1: pzp \to out$
    $C_{out}: out \to 0$
    This only captures the positive half-cycle. The negative half-cycle is wasted.
    To capture the negative half-cycle, you need the other diodes.
    So FBR is better.

    Let's try a second topology just in case.
    Design 2: SSHI but with a different switch configuration? No, Parallel-SSHI is the most common.
    What about a "Synchronous Rectifier"?
    Replacing the diodes with switches.
    $S_1: pzp \to out$
    $S_2: pzn \to out$
    $S_3: 0 \to pzp$
    $S_4: 0 \to pzn$
    But we only have 4 switches total, and we need some for the flip.
    Also, the SYNC controllers are limited to 2.
    So we can't have a full synchronous rectifier and an SSHI flip.

    Design 2: "Cold-start optimized".
    What if we use a smaller $C_{out}$ to speed up $t_{up}$, but then ripple increases?
    The problem is $V_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$.
    Maybe a larger $L$ for better energy transfer?

    Let's stick with one strong proposal for now: the Parallel-SSHI with Zener Clamp.
    Actually, I can provide a few variations of it as different "topologies" (e.g., different ways to implement the rectifier).

    Wait, the prompt says "up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity".
    So I can't just change $L$ or $C$.

    Topology 1: SSHI + Full-Bridge + Zener.
    Topology 2: SSHI + Half-Bridge (by grounding $pzn$).
    Wait, if I ground $pzn$, then $pzn$ is no longer a node I can use for the switch $S_1$.
    $S_1$ would be $pzp \to 0$ through $L$.
    Let's see:
    Piezo between $pzp$ and $0$ (by connecting $pzn \to 0$).
    $D_1: pzp \to out$
    $D_2: pzp \to 0$ (Not helpful)
    No, if $pzn$ is $0$, you still need a full bridge or a capacitor to capture the negative cycle.
    Actually, the standard half-bridge rectifier is:
    $pzp \to D_1 \to out$
    $pzp \to C_1 \to 0$
    But we can't add a big capacitor in series with the piezo easily.

    Let's try Topology 2: SSHI with a "Voltage Doubler" (Charge Pump) rectifier.
    $D_1: pzp \to n1$
    $C_1: n1 \to 0$
    $D_2: n1 \to out$
    $C_{out}: out \to 0$
    (This is for a single-ended source).
    But we have a differential source ($pzp, pzn$).
    A differential charge pump:
    $D_1: pzp \to n1$
    $D_2: pzn \to n1$
    $C_1: n1 \to 0$
    $D_3: n1 \to out$
    Wait, that's not a doubler.

    Let's stick to the SSHI + FBR + Zener. It's the most reliable.
    What if I try a different SSHI variant?
    "Series-SSHI" uses a switch to connect the piezo to the storage capacitor.
    But that's more complex.

    One more thought: $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$.
    If the FBR has $V_{pp} = 83\text{ mV}$ for S2, and we use SSHI, the energy per pulse is higher, but the frequency is the same. $C_{out}$ is the main lever for $V_{pp}$.
    $C_{out} = 4.7\text{ uF}$ should be enough.

    *   L1: 10mH
    *   Cout: 4.7uF
    *   S1: pzp -> n1
    *   L1: n1 -> pzn
    *   G1: ton=1.5e-4, edges=both, phase=0
    *   D1-D4: FBR
    *   Dz: Zener (0 -> out)

    Wait, let me check the $T_{on}$ again.
    $T_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    $C_p$ varies from $17.5\text{ nF}$ to $32.5\text{ nF}$.
    For $17.5\text{ nF}, L=10\text{mH} \to T_{on} = 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 1.75 \cdot 10^{-8}}$... no.
    $L=10\text{mH} = 10^{-2} \text{ H}$.
    $\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 2.5 \cdot 10^{-8}} = \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5}$.
    $T_{on} = 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-5} \text{ s}$.
    My previous calculation was wrong. $L=10\text{mH}$ is a good starting point.

    Wait, if I have 16 components:
    - 4 Diodes (FBR)
    - 1 Diode (Zener)
    - 1 Capacitor (Cout)
    - 1 Inductor (L1)
    - 1 Switch (S1)
    - 1 SYNC (G1)
    Total = 9 components. I have plenty of room.

    Let's consider if I should add another capacitor for better filtering?
    No, one large $C_{out}$ is usually enough for piezo.

    What about the "settled" $dV \le 0.02\text{ V}$?
    This means the output must be very stable. A larger $C_{out}$ helps.

    Wait, I should check if there's any way to improve $t_{up}$ further.
    A smaller $C_{out}$ would start faster, but then $V_{pp}$ and $dV$ would fail.
    The SSHI's energy boost is the primary way to fix $t_{up}$.
